Generative language modeling for antibody CDR grafting and alignment-driven de novo design

1. The paper introduces GenCDR, a framework-first autoregressive (LLaMA-style) antibody language model: it reads all framework regions (FR1–FR4) as the prompt, then generates all CDRs jointly as a variable-length response, creating a clean prompt–response boundary for reward attribution and alignment.

2. This re-ordering directly targets the core de novo antibody problem as an infilling task: CDR design conditioned on a fixed scaffold. Unlike left-to-right decoding (where early CDRs lack downstream framework context), GenCDR generates CDRs with full framework context available from the start.

3. GenCDR is presented as a model family covering common design settings: IgGenCDR (unpaired human OAS, ~254M sequences), p-IgGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~1.8M natively paired VH–VL sequences), and NanoGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~6.5M camelid VHH from INDI plus human OAS heavy chains in a 1:1 mixture to preserve humanness on humanized scaffolds).

4. On CDR recovery (next-token prediction accuracy over CDR tokens) using a CDR3-disjoint held-out test set designed to reduce leakage, framework-first ordering improves over a same-sized left-to-right ablation and surpasses prior autoregressive baselines (including p-IgGen, ProGen2-OAS, and IgLM) across essentially all loops, with especially strong gains where downstream context matters most (e.g., CDR1).

5. De novo generation quality: when prompted with held-out frameworks and sampling CDRs jointly, GenCDR reproduces natural CDR length distributions closely (across all loops), while maintaining human-likeness (OASis), naturalness (ESM-2 PLL), and diversity/novelty with smooth trade-offs across sampling temperatures.

6. A key design consequence of the framework-first factorization is separable CDR likelihoods: GenCDR can score only the generated CDR block (rather than conflating framework+CDR likelihood), enabling clearer optimization targets and more principled alignment for CDR-centric objectives.

7. Likelihoods retain useful biological signal: GenCDR log-likelihood correlates zero-shot with experimental fitness/developability benchmarks (FLAb). The analysis also highlights assay locality: immunogenicity appears more CDR-driven, while expression is more framework-driven, and paired scoring (p-IgGenCDR) improves correlations when heavy+light are scored jointly.

8. NanoGenCDR extends the framework-first approach to nanobodies: fine-tuning closes the human→camelid distribution shift in CDR recovery, generates plausible/developable VHHs (including fold-confidence and developability flag rates comparable to reference), and improves humanness on humanized VHH scaffolds specifically due to the camelid+human mixture strategy.

9. Alignment-driven de novo design: the prompt–response boundary enables iterative alignment with weighted DPO (wDPO) using rewards computed only on the generated CDR completion. They optimize a composite reward from antibody–antigen co-folding metrics (Boltz-2) plus non-differentiable developability liability rules, demonstrating multi-objective steering without explicit antigen encoding in the model input.

10. In a PD-L1 nanobody design benchmark, four rounds of alignment drive near-perfect compliance with length/liability constraints after one round (acceptance ~23.8% → ~99.8–100%), and achieve in silico interface metrics competitive with a structure-conditioned diffusion pipeline (BoltzGen) at roughly half the sampling budget, while producing sequences that remain more “natural” under independent language-model scoring—suggesting KL-anchored alignment can push target-facing metrics without excessive distributional drift.

[📃 PAPER ALERT] Efficient, Property-Aligned Fan-Out Retrieval via RL-Compiled Diffusion - by Google Research & UIUC
arXiv: https://t.co/tt5pGCsbU3

When we search something broad like “camping gear,” we don't really want 10 slightly different tents.

We want:
tent + sleeping bag + stove + headlamp + other complementary things.
So modern search systems use query fan-out: take one broad query --> generate multiple sub-queries --> retrieve different aspects of the user's intent.

Sounds simple.

But there is a problem.

LLMs are autoregressive. To generate a good set of complementary, diverse AND database-grounded queries, they may need expensive inference-time reasoning.

And for a search system... do we really want the model to “think” heavily every single time someone searches?

I think NO.

This paper proposes : Retrieve-for-Train.

The idea is actually quite interesting:

Use expensive RL during TRAINING, not during INFERENCE.

The pipeline has 3 stages:

Train a Fan-Out Language Model (FOLM) using RL to generate useful sub-queries.

The reward jointly optimizes:

a. Groundedness: are the queries actually connected to items in the database?
b. Alignment: do they still follow the user's original intent?
c. Diversity: do they explore genuinely different semantic directions?

Use this RL-trained model to generate synthetic supervision.
So the expensive exploration happens offline.
No human-labelled property-aligned dataset is required.

Train a lightweight diffusion retriever on these generated targets.

At inference time, instead of autoregressively generating query after query...

the diffusion model generates multiple retrieval directions in parallel in embedding space.

Basically:

RL discovers the search strategy --> synthetic data stores it --> diffusion executes it cheaply.

Findings:
1. Zero-shot query fan-out helps, but it is not enough.
Normal LLMs often generate near-identical queries.
R4T instead learns complementary directions that cover more of the semantic space.
2. R4T improves retrieval quality over zero-shot fan-out and Best-of-N baselines.
The method was evaluated on fashion and music retrieval tasks where the desired output is a set rather than one correct item.
3. The diffusion retriever makes fan-out dramatically cheaper.

Their 53.9M-parameter diffusion model generates the retrieval directions non-autoregressively.

Reported fan-out latency:

LLM: ~1.46 s → ~50 s as batch size grows
Diffusion: ~0.07 s → 4.21 s

That is roughly 12×–20× faster.

[Interestingly]
The diversity reward is doing something more important than simply making the results diverse.

Without it, the RL model can reward-hack.

Optimizing only groundedness can produce nonsense strings that happen to land close to database embeddings.
Adding alignment alone can instead make the model collapse into repetitive paraphrases.

Groundedness + Alignment + Diversity work like counter-anchors that prevent these shortcuts.

I found this part particularly interesting because it shows how important reward interaction is in RL-based retrieval.

[In short] Instead of asking a large model to solve the same difficult search problem again and again at inference time...solve it during training and compile the learned behavior into a smaller model.

So the idea is almost:
System-2-like exploration during training → System-1-like retrieval during deployment.
And I think the broader idea may be even more interesting than retrieval itself.
Can we use RL to discover expensive behaviors once, turn those behaviors into training data, and then deploy a much cheaper model that reproduces them?

**Holding AI to the Truth: Why Blockchain Matters** (written with assistance from @Grok.  

Artificial intelligence is extraordinary at producing fluent answers. It is less reliable at producing *settled* ones. On occasion — more often than casual users admit — models *hallucinate*: they invent citations, invent facts, invent confidence. The output can look authoritative and still be wrong. That is not a moral failing of the machine; it is a property of probabilistic generation without a shared ledger of what actually happened.

In July 2019, on Real Vision with Raoul Pal (@RaoulGMI) macro investor Dan Tapiero (@DTAPCAP) named the other half of this problem years before “AI agents” entered every pitch deck. Bitcoin, he argued, is not merely a coin. It is an *invention* — and at its core, “a truth machine”: a system bought for “certainty, of confirmation, of validity, of security,” a platform with a track record that makes fraud and silent revision harder. He later sharpened the phrase to “security truth machine.” (Popular memory sometimes upgrades that to “automatic truth machine”; the idea is the same.)

The distinction that matters for AI is precise. A blockchain does not magically know whether a claim about the physical world is true. It does not replace science, journalism, or judgment. What it *does* provide is **immutable, shared state**: who signed what, who paid whom, which model version ran, which data hash was used, which action an agent took and when. Once written under consensus rules, that record is extremely hard for any single party — including an AI system acting on someone’s behalf — to rewrite quietly.

That is exactly the property generative models lack. An LLM can narrate a trade that never settled, a contract that was never signed, a medical note that was never reviewed. An agent economy that scales without rails for settlement, identity, and audit is an economy of plausible fiction at machine speed. Tokenized dollars, on-chain credentials, and programmable settlement are not crypto fashion statements in that frame; they are **truth infrastructure for machine actors**.

Tapiero’s 2019 insight travels forward cleanly into the AI decade. The internet digitized information. Crypto digitizes value *and* verifiable record. If artificial intelligence is going to operate as a participant in markets, payments, and institutions — not merely as a chatbot — then “holding AI to the truth” cannot mean hoping the next model is nicer. It means binding machine action to ledgers that do not hallucinate their own history.

Blockchain is not the answer to every truth. It is the answer to a narrower, more urgent one: **who did what, with what authority, and can anyone erase the receipt?** In a world of confident machines, that receipt is not optional.

—
*Source: Tapiero × Raoul Pal, Real Vision “The Future of Macro Investing” (~Jul 2019), ~00:09:46 — “What it really is, is it’s a truth machine.” https://t.co/JxTkN4pGjO*

Train frontier models with reinforcement learning at scale!

Miles is an open-source framework for large-scale RL post-training across LLMs and VLMs.

At this scale, RL is not just about choosing an algorithm like GRPO or PPO. You also need fast rollouts, distributed training, weight synchronization, memory management, and a way to keep the training data aligned with what the model actually generated.

Miles brings those pieces together.

SGLang handles high-throughput rollouts, while Megatron-LM or FSDP2 handles training. Rollout and training can run asynchronously, so generation does not have to stop every time the model updates.

For long multi-turn or tool-using trajectories, Miles also preserves the exact token IDs produced during rollout before feeding them back into training. For MoE models, it can replay the expert-routing decisions from rollout during training to reduce mismatch between the two stages.

The system is built for very large models too.

In one reference setup, Miles runs asynchronous RL training for a 744B model across 64 GB300 GPUs. Its P2P weight synchronization also reduced the update time for a 1T-parameter Kimi-K2 setup from 53.3 seconds to 7.2 seconds.

Key capabilities:

• Fully asynchronous RL training
• SGLang rollouts with Megatron-LM or FSDP2 training
• GRPO, GSPO, PPO, REINFORCE++, SFT, and distillation
• Token-faithful training for multi-turn trajectories
• MoE routing replay between rollout and training
• CPU and NVMe optimizer-state offloading
• NVIDIA and AMD GPU support
• Agentic RL and sandboxed environments

It also extends beyond language models, with a separate Miles-Diffusion stack for RL post-training of diffusion models.

100% open source.

this 15-second fashion clip starts with spilled coffee and ends with physics giving up.

a woman loses control of her phone, cup, and glasses.

that progression is not random.

it is built around a repeatable attention structure:

1. GPT-6 Astra finds videos performing far above their creators' normal reach.
2. it isolates the opening, escalation, visual interruption, and replay moment.
3. Picsart's AI director Lina rebuilds those mechanics around a new subject and maps every shot before generation begins.
4. the original footage and characters are replaced while the proven viewing pattern remains.
5. Make publishes each version across Shorts, Reels, and TikTok, then sends the retention data into the next research pass.

the complete setup took two hours and costs $44 per month.

the real advantage is not making one impossible clip.

it is having a process that can design the next 100 without returning to a blank page.
